name: Graphs
tagline: Visit each node once. BFS finds the fewest steps.

blocks.html:
A city map: places are nodes, roads are edges. A grid is a graph too: each cell links to its four neighbors.

Most graph questions are a walk that visits each node once and remembers what it has seen.

blocks.text: Example: fewest steps across a grid

blocks.note: Try every path, then BFS in rings from the start

blocks.html: BFS explores in rings: everything 1 step away, then 2, then 3. So the first time you reach a cell is along a shortest path, and you never need to visit it again.

blocks.q: Why mark a cell as seen when you enqueue it, not when you pop it?
options: It stops the same cell entering the queue many times
BFS would return the wrong distance
blocks.why: If you mark late, several neighbors can each add the same cell before it is popped. The answer stays right, but the queue and the work grow.

pitfalls: Mark visited when you enqueue, or the queue fills with duplicates.
Recursive DFS on a big grid can pass Python's recursion limit. Use BFS or an explicit stack.
